title: SYSK Tribute: Why does everyone love Dolly Parton?
summary: Tribute rerun of a 2023 Stuff You Should Know episode, reposted the day after Dolly Parton's death, asking why so many people love her. The hosts trace her life from a large, poor Smoky Mountains childhood in Sevier County, Tennessee, through her early recordings, her work with Porter Wagoner, and her solo success with "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You." They cover her 1970s and 1980s crossover pop hits, her acting and songwriting, Dollywood and its museum, her public image and fan base (including LGBTQ and Black women audiences), her political neutrality, business dealings, philanthropy and the Imagination Library, awards, and listener mail about a grandmother who was a Pac-Man player.

segments.title: Tribute release intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this 2023 episode as a tribute, released the day after Dolly Parton's death from cancer, and explains why she was so widely beloved.

segments.title: Opening banter on why everyone loves Dolly
segments.summary: The hosts discuss her Rolling Stone interview, her refusal to get into politics, her broad appeal across political lines, and the Dolly Parton's America podcast series by Jad Abumrad.

segments.title: Childhood in the Smoky Mountains
segments.summary: Dolly Parton was born in January 1946 in Sevier County, Tennessee, the fourth of 12 children, raised in a two-room cabin. Her uncle Bill Owens nurtured her musical talent, and she wrote her first song at age five.

segments.title: Early recordings and move to Nashville
segments.summary: Her first recording, Puppy Love, came in 1959 when she was 13, and she debuted at the Grand Ole Opry introduced by Johnny Cash. She signed with Mercury Records in 1962 and moved to Nashville the day after high school graduation in 1964. She met her husband Carl Dean at a laundromat.

segments.title: Monument Records and debut album
segments.summary: Dolly signed with Monument Records in 1965, where they wanted her to be a pop singer, but she insisted on country. Her 1967 debut album Hello, I'm Dolly included the top 20 country hits Dumb Blonde and Something Fishy.

segments.title: Working with Porter Wagoner
segments.summary: Porter Wagoner hired Dolly for his syndicated show, and their duets and albums including Just Between You and Me in 1968 made the show a top syndicated program. He kept tight control through exploitive contracts. She later left him, wrote I Will Always Love You about the split, and reconciled before his death.
topics: I Will Always Love You origin

segments.title: Solo career, Jolene, and breaking away
segments.summary: Dolly released many solo albums while still with Wagoner, writing Jolene and I Will Always Love You around the same time. She left Wagoner, reportedly with his permission to release the song, despite his breach-of-contract suit, and replaced her family band. She hosted a variety show called Dolly in 1976-77.

segments.title: Sandy Gallen and crossover pop success
segments.summary: Manager Sandy Gallen, who was gay, booked her at the Bottom Line in Greenwich Village, took her to Europe, and helped her crossover. Her hit Here You Come Again went number one on the country chart and number three on pop, and the album went platinum. Her TV appearances in the 1970s and 1980s made her a household name.

segments.title: Later albums, collaborations, Christmas music, and songwriting
segments.summary: Dolly collaborated with Kenny Rogers on Islands in the Stream and recorded the 1987 album Trio with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris. She also released bluegrass albums and Christmas albums, and she describes songwriting as her proudest achievement, often writing from a male point of view.

segments.title: Dollywood origins and the museum
segments.summary: Jack and Pete Herschend of Silver Dollar City in Pigeon Forge reached out after Dolly mentioned a home theme park in a 1982 Barbara Walters interview. Dollywood opened four years later and drew 1.3 million visitors in its first year. A time capsule with an unreleased Dolly song is buried there. The hosts describe the museum, which holds her coat of many colors and her career lists, and nearby Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge attractions.

segments.title: Public image, Q score, and political stance
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sociologist Tressie McMillan Cottom on Black women's admiration, Dolly's legendary Q score, the anthropologist Jonathan Zilberg's work on her popularity in Zimbabwe, and Nelson Mandela's reported use of Jolene in prison. They note she avoids partisan politics, supports causes like Black Lives Matter, changed the Dixie Stampede name in 2018, and jokes about her own image. Her feminism and dark songs such as Daddy Come and Get Me are also covered.

segments.title: Business, philanthropy, and literacy
segments.summary: Dolly kept rights to her music, refusing Elvis Presley's demand for half the publishing of I Will Always Love You. Her catalog and Dollywood stake make her wealthy. She licenses her image for products like Duncan Hines frosting. Her Dollywood Foundation, begun in 1988, has given away more than 204 million books, and she donated $1 million to Vanderbilt for COVID-19 vaccine research.

segments.title: Awards, records, and upcoming projects
segments.summary: Dolly has been nominated for 53 Grammys and won 10, with Jolene and I Will Always Love You in the Grammy Hall of Fame. She was Oscar-nominated for Traveling Through and 9 to 5, holds two Guinness records and two Hollywood Walk of Fame stars, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Her album Rockstar was announced.

segments.title: Listener mail: grandmother and Pac-Man
segments.summary: Listener Aaron Miller of Kansas City writes about his grandmother, a homemaker who secretly played Pac-Man and reached the level 256 kill screen before anyone else knew of it.
